nodes.title: Splunk SPL (Splunk Core Certified User/Power User): Key Ideas
nodes.content: SPL (Search Processing Language) is Splunk's query language. The Splunk Core exam tests the search pipeline, statistical commands (`stats`, `chart`, `timechart`), field extraction with `rex`, deduplication, transaction grouping, and lookup enrichment — all composable in a left-to-right pipe syntax.

flashcards.front: What is the SPL search pipeline?
flashcards.back: SPL is a sequence of commands separated by `|`. Results flow left to right: each command transforms the output of the previous. Example: `index=web status=404 | stats count by uri | sort -count | head 10`. The first segment (before the first `|`) is the search command that retrieves events from the index; subsequent pipes refine, aggregate, or format those events.

flashcards.front: stats vs chart vs timechart — what does each produce?
flashcards.back: `stats`: aggregate over all results into a flat table — `stats count, avg(bytes) by status`. `chart`: produce a table with one row per value of the BY clause and columns per OVER clause — good for cross-tabulations. `timechart`: time-bucketed aggregation with _time on the X-axis — `timechart span=1h avg(response_ms) by host`. Use timechart for trend charts in dashboards.

flashcards.front: What does `rex` do and when do you need it?
flashcards.back: `rex` extracts fields using a named capture group regex inline during search — e.g., `rex field=_raw "user=(?<username>\w+)"` creates a `username` field without modifying the source data. Use it when a field you need isn't already extracted by a field extraction (props.conf/transforms.conf). For permanent extraction, define it in transforms.conf; for ad-hoc exploration, use `rex`.

flashcards.front: transaction vs stats — when do you use transaction?
flashcards.back: `transaction` groups related events into a single event based on shared field values and/or time gaps — e.g., `transaction session_id maxspan=30m` groups all web events for the same session. It preserves raw event content and adds `duration` and `eventcount` fields. Use it when you need the full raw events; use `stats` when you only need aggregated values — `stats` is orders of magnitude faster at scale.

nodes.title: Splunk knowledge objects (Splunk Core): Key Ideas
nodes.content: Knowledge objects are the building blocks of Splunk data enrichment: field aliases rename existing fields, calculated fields derive new ones, event types classify events, tags add metadata, macros define reusable search snippets, and data models power Pivot and Accelerated search. The Core exam tests what each object does and the order in which Splunk applies them.

flashcards.front: Field alias vs calculated field — what is the difference?
flashcards.back: Field alias: creates an alternate name for an existing extracted field — `clientip` aliased as `src_ip`. No data is duplicated; both names point to the same value. Calculated field: creates a brand-new field whose value is derived by an `eval` expression — `response_kb = bytes / 1024`. Calculated fields require the source field(s) to already exist; they add a derived column.

flashcards.front: Event types vs tags — how do they differ?
flashcards.back: Event type: a saved search that classifies events matching its criteria — e.g., `index=web status>=400` is the `http_errors` event type. Any event matching it gets the `eventtype=http_errors` field. Tags: user-defined labels attached to specific field=value pairs — e.g., tag the value `status=404` with the tag `not_found`. Tags and event types both enrich events; event types are search-based classification, tags are value-based labeling.

flashcards.front: Macros — what problem do they solve?
flashcards.back: Macros are saved SPL snippets (optionally with arguments) that can be referenced in any search using backtick syntax: `` `web_errors` `` expands to the full search string defined in the macro. They solve DRY violations — if your team writes the same 40-character filter in 50 searches, a macro means you change it in one place. Arguments (`macro(arg1,arg2)`) make macros reusable across different index names, timeframes, etc.

flashcards.front: Data models and CIM — what is each?
flashcards.back: Data model: a hierarchical schema that describes the expected fields and constraints for a type of data (Web, Network Traffic, Authentication) — the foundation for Pivot UI and accelerated searches. CIM (Common Information Model): Splunk's standard data model library with normalized field names across data sources — `src_ip`, `dest_ip`, `action` instead of vendor-specific names. CIM compliance means every app speaks the same field language, enabling cross-source correlation.

nodes.title: Troubleshooting methodology: Key Ideas
nodes.content: A structured troubleshooting process beats random guessing every time. The classic flow: identify the problem precisely, form a theory, test it, fix, verify, document. Most exams test that you know the flow AND can spot the layer at which the symptom originates.

flashcards.front: What's the standard troubleshooting model?
flashcards.back: CompTIA's 6-step: (1) Identify the problem (gather symptoms, questions to user, recent changes). (2) Establish a theory of probable cause. (3) Test the theory. (4) Plan and implement the fix. (5) Verify full system functionality, apply preventive measures. (6) Document everything.

flashcards.front: Top-down vs bottom-up troubleshooting on a network problem.
flashcards.back: Top-down: start at the application layer and work down — does the browser work? DNS? TCP? Routing? Bottom-up: start at the physical layer — is the cable plugged in? Link light? IP? When you suspect physical/cable, bottom-up is faster. When the user has 'a website is broken', top-down is faster.

flashcards.front: Why ask 'what changed recently'?
flashcards.back: Almost every production incident traces back to a recent change — a deploy, a config push, a vendor patch, a cert rotation. 'It was working yesterday' tells you to check today's change-log before forming an exotic theory. Recent changes are the highest-priors of the bug space.

flashcards.front: What's the divide-and-conquer technique?
flashcards.back: Bisect the path between symptom and cause. If 10 hops between client and server, test hop 5. Good → problem is past hop 5. Bad → problem is before. Two more bisections narrow it to one hop. Faster than checking every link sequentially when the chain is long.

questions.q: An analyst wants to ENRICH search results with data from an external CSV (`asset_owners.csv`) — joining on a key field. The CSV is loaded as a Splunk knowledge object that can be referenced in searches. Plus a SPL command lets you load the CSV contents directly into the search pipeline (no event correlation, just rows). Which describes Splunk lookups + `inputlookup`?
choices: Lookups enrich events with data from external CSV/KV/Geo sources, joining on a key field
Lookups map index names to labels using an external reference table; `inputlookup` lists all defined lookups and can enrich events by index label
Lookups are field-alias tables that enrich events by joining on external alias mappings; `inputlookup` shows those mappings
Lookups are saved searches that enrich results by joining on external criteria at schedule time; `inputlookup` runs them on demand
questions.explanation: A Splunk lookup enriches events with additional fields by matching a lookup key field to rows in an external CSV or KV store. The `lookup` command performs this enrichment mid-search. The `inputlookup` command reads the entire lookup table as a search result set, useful for inspecting or joining lookup data directly. inputlookup reads the lookup file as a search source

questions.q: Splunk supports AUTOMATIC LOOKUPS: a lookup configured in `Settings → Lookups → Automatic lookups` so it's applied to EVERY search against a specified host / source / sourcetype WITHOUT requiring `| lookup …` in the SPL. Which describes this?
choices: A lookup that is configured as a scheduled saved search and automatically applied to enrich results on each scheduled run — that is a saved-search + outputlookup combination, not automatic lookup

A lookup configured with an auto-refresh interval in Settings that periodically re-reads the CSV and applies updated values to future searches — that describes KV Store collection refresh, not automatic lookup
A lookup configured in Settings → Lookups → Automatic Lookups that is automatically applied to search results when an event contains the lookup's input field
A lookup that is automatically applied when writing new entries, auto-creating records for each unique field value encountered — lookups are read-only by default and do not auto-write
questions.explanation: An automatic lookup (configured in Settings > Lookups > Automatic Lookups) is applied automatically at search time whenever events contain the lookup's input field — without requiring `| lookup` in the search string. This is useful for enriching events at index time or universally, such as automatically adding hostname from IP using a DNS lookup table.

questions.q: An analyst wants every event with a `host` field to be ENRICHED at search time with the host's owner + criticality from a KV-store collection `cmdb_hosts`. The enrichment should happen AUTOMATICALLY for the entire app's searches — no need to type `| lookup` each time. Which feature?
choices: Automatic lookup pointing to a KV-store collection
Real-time search with subsearch
Data model acceleration
Workflow action
questions.explanation: KV Store lookups work just like CSV lookups but store data in a MongoDB-compatible key-value store. An automatic lookup configured to use a KV Store collection enriches events at search time automatically. KV Store lookups support larger datasets and allow CRUD operations via REST API and Splunk's `outputlookup`/`inputlookup` commands.

questions.q: A scheduled saved-search computes daily aggregates and PERSISTS the results to a CSV lookup file `daily_totals.csv`. Subsequent dashboards read from the CSV via `| inputlookup daily_totals.csv`. The pipe that WRITES the search's current results into the lookup is `| outputlookup daily_totals.csv`. Which describes `outputlookup`?
choices: `inputlookup daily_summary.csv` — reads current records from a CSV lookup file into the search pipeline for joining or enrichment; the opposite direction from `outputlookup` writes
`outputlookup daily_summary.csv` — writes current search results to a CSV lookup file, replacing or appending the file's contents
`outputcsv daily_summary` — writes current search results to a standard CSV export; `outputcsv` is not a valid SPL command for lookup files
`dbxlookup daily_summary` — writes current search results to an external database via a lookup definition; requires the DB Connect app and a different syntax
questions.explanation: `outputlookup` writes search results to a CSV file or KV Store lookup table. This is used to create or update lookup files programmatically. For example, running a daily search that outputs a list of known bad IPs to a CSV, which is then used by `lookup` to enrich future events. Requires write permission on the lookup.

questions.q: An analyst runs `| lookup customers customer_id AS user_id OUTPUT name` but gets ZERO matched rows even though the CSV has matching entries. The CSV has a column `customer_id` and events have `user_id`. Most likely cause?
choices: The CSV lookup file was modified externally and its customer_id column header was changed, so the output field name mapping no longer takes effect

The lookup's input field name in the lookup definition (`customer_id`) doesn't match the event field name (`user_id`) — using `AS user_id` aliases the event field but the lookup definition still expects `customer_id` as the output key

CSV lookups cannot perform case-sensitive customer_id name matching, so rows whose `name` output values contain mixed case are silently dropped — case-sensitivity is configurable in the lookup definition and is not the cause of zero matches here

The lookup file is too large and was truncated during upload, dropping all rows that contain the customer_id and `name` output fields — the zero-match symptom here is a field name mismatch, not file truncation
questions.explanation: The most common cause of lookup returning 0 enrichment results is a mismatch between the input field name in the lookup definition and the field name that actually exists in the events. For example, if the lookup definition specifies input field `src_ip` but events have the field as `src`, the lookup won't find matches. Check the field name exactly. Case sensitivity of values is the second most common issue (default lookups are case-sensitive).

nodes.title: Observability and monitoring: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Observability is metrics + logs + traces — the three pillars. You need all three to debug a production incident: metrics tell you something is wrong, logs tell you what happened, traces tell you where in the call graph the problem lives.

flashcards.front: Metrics vs logs vs traces — what does each tell you?
flashcards.back: Metrics: numeric time-series, cheap to store, perfect for dashboards and alerts ('p99 latency = 800 ms'). Logs: discrete events with context, expensive at scale, perfect for forensics. Traces: causally-linked spans showing a request's full path through services.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between an alert and a notification?
flashcards.back: An alert is a condition that fires when a metric crosses a threshold (CPU > 80% for 5 min). The notification is the resulting message (email, Slack, PagerDuty page). One alert can fan out to many notifications. Tuning alerts is harder than wiring notifications.

flashcards.front: What is an SLI / SLO / SLA?
flashcards.back: SLI (indicator): the metric you actually measure ('% of requests under 200 ms'). SLO (objective): the internal target ('99.9% of requests under 200 ms over 28 days'). SLA (agreement): the contractual promise to customers, usually weaker than the SLO so you have buffer.

flashcards.front: Why structured logs?
flashcards.back: Plain-text logs are unparseable at scale. Structured logs (JSON, with timestamp + level + service + request_id + key fields) are indexable, queryable, and join-able across services. Most platforms auto-extract fields from JSON without configuration.

questions.q: An admin sets up an alert: 'fire when the COUNT of failed logins from a single IP exceeds 10 in any rolling 15-minute window'. The Splunk alert condition selector lets them pick the trigger type. Which option fits?
choices: Number of events > 10 — refers to raw event count, not the aggregated `stats count by src_ip` result rows
Number of results > 10
Custom condition: `count > 10` — works but rendered as 'Number of Results' in the UI
Number of hosts > 10 — counts distinct hosts, wrong dimension here (IPs)
questions.explanation: For a stats-based search like `stats count by src_ip | where count > 10`, the alert trigger 'Number of results > 0' fires when any row passes the `where` filter. If using a raw event count without stats, use 'Number of events > 10'. The key distinction: 'results' counts rows in a table, 'events' counts raw events in a non-transforming search.

questions.q: An admin compares two Splunk artefacts. SCHEDULED REPORTS run on a cron schedule + emit results; ALERTS are scheduled reports PLUS a TRIGGER CONDITION (`if number of results > 10 then …`) that fires email / webhook / script. Which describes the difference?
choices: Scheduled reports trigger actions when their schedule fires; alerts trigger actions only by email
Both run on a schedule
Alerts save their schedule results to a CSV; reports display results in dashboards
Alerts run on a continuous real-time schedule; reports run on a cron schedule
questions.explanation: Both scheduled reports and alerts run on a schedule. The key difference is that alerts include trigger conditions that evaluate the search results and only fire an action (email, PagerDuty, run script, etc.) when the condition is met (e.g., number of results > 0). Scheduled reports always run and generate results but don't trigger conditional actions — they are used for generating recurring reports.

questions.q: An alert fires on every 5-minute schedule whenever the trigger condition is met. The ops team gets spammed with duplicate emails. The admin enables THROTTLING with `suppress for 1 hour by src_ip` — after firing for an IP, the alert won't re-fire for the SAME IP for 1 hour. What does THROTTLE do?
choices: Throttle suppresses the alert from firing until a minimum number of trigger events accumulate in the alert results — that is the alert trigger condition threshold, not throttling
Throttle reduces the alert's search schedule frequency so the cron trigger fires less often to lower resource consumption — that is the alert cron schedule setting, not throttling
Throttle limits the number of events returned in the alert results to a fixed count using the same logic as the `head` command — that is result limiting, not alert suppression
Throttle suppresses re-firing of the alert for a specified period (optionally per field value), preventing duplicate notifications when the alert condition persists
questions.explanation: Alert throttling suppresses the alert from firing again for a configurable time window (e.g., 24 hours) after it first triggers, to prevent alert fatigue. You can throttle on a specific field value — for example, throttle for 1 hour per unique `src_ip` so the same attacker IP only triggers one alert per hour instead of one per 5-minute search cycle.

questions.q: A Splunk alert has two scheduling modes. (Real-time) the alert search runs CONTINUOUSLY on a rolling time window (e.g., last 5 min) and trigger conditions are evaluated on every result update — most timely but most resource-heavy. (Scheduled) the alert search runs on a CRON schedule (every N minutes), trigger conditions evaluated after each completion — cheaper but less timely. Which describes Real-time vs Scheduled?
choices: Real-time alerts incur heavy overhead but support timely email notifications only; scheduled alerts support all action types
Real-time alerts fire every second and are therefore as heavy as scheduled alerts for short intervals
Real-time alerts use streaming-only evaluation on new events; scheduled alerts search historical data only
Real-time = continuous rolling-window evaluation (most timely, resource-heavy)
questions.explanation: Real-time alerts in Splunk continuously evaluate a rolling time window (e.g., always looking at the last 5 minutes of data). The trigger condition is checked as new events arrive. Scheduled alerts run the search at specific intervals (every 15 minutes, hourly, etc.) and check results at that point in time. Real-time alerts are resource-intensive and generally reserved for high-priority use cases. Scheduled runs the search at defined intervals

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.
